topic.title: SLOs and Reliability — error budgets and resilient AI services

outcomes: Define user-centered SLIs for availability, latency, freshness and task quality in an AI application.
Calculate SLO attainment, error budgets, budget consumption and multi-window burn rates from explicit denominators.
Design request deadlines, bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, retry budgets and idempotency for side effects.
Implement circuit breakers, bulkheads, backpressure and graceful degradation for model, retrieval and tool dependencies.
Separate infrastructure availability from AI quality and safety objectives, and choose alerts that reflect user impact.
Build deterministic reliability simulations and failure-injection tests for provider outages, slow responses, queue saturation and recovery.
prerequisites: Basic probability, percentiles, HTTP timeouts and distributed systems

glossary.definition: A measurable service indicator that represents a user-visible reliability dimension such as successful requests or latency.
A target value for an SLI over a defined measurement window, such as 99.9% successful requests over 30 days.
An external agreement that may define service commitments, remedies and exclusions; it is not interchangeable with an internal SLO.
The allowed amount of SLI failure during an SLO window, calculated from the target and eligible event count.
The rate at which observed bad events consume the allowed error budget relative to the target rate.
A state machine that temporarily stops calls to a failing dependency and later permits controlled recovery probes.
Isolation of concurrency, queues or resources so one overloaded dependency cannot exhaust the entire service.
A signal or admission-control mechanism that slows or rejects upstream work when downstream capacity is exhausted.
A controlled reduced-capability response that remains safe and understandable when optional dependencies fail.

explanation.problem: AI applications depend on model providers, embedding services, vector databases, tool APIs, queues and storage. A provider outage or slow dependency can cascade through retries and queues, exhausting resources and turning a partial failure into a platform-wide outage. Without user-centered SLOs, teams either alert on noise or discover reliability problems through customer complaints.
explanation.plainLanguage:
Start with what the user experiences, not whether a server process is running. An availability SLI might count eligible requests that return a valid response within a deadline. A latency SLI might measure the proportion of requests completed under two seconds, or p95 latency. A RAG system may also need freshness and task-quality indicators. Keep infrastructure reliability, model quality and safety as related but distinct objectives: a fast response can still be wrong or unsafe.

An SLO is a target over a window. If the target is 99.5% successful requests, the error budget is 0.5% of eligible requests. For 10,000 eligible requests, that allows 50 bad requests. If 80 fail, the budget is exceeded. Define the denominator carefully: decide how to treat invalid client requests, health checks, cancellations, internal retries and synthetic probes. Do not exclude real user-visible failures just because a dependency was external.

Burn rate compares the observed failure ratio with the allowed failure ratio. If the SLO permits 0.5% bad events and a recent window has 2% bad events, the burn rate is 4x. Alert on multi-window burn rates so a fast budget drain pages quickly while a sustained slower regression creates a lower-severity signal. Error budgets are a decision tool: when consumed rapidly, pause risky releases, prioritize reliability work and reduce optional load.

Reliability begins with deadlines. Propagate one end-to-end deadline through retrieval, model and tool calls; do not give every downstream service a fresh full timeout. Retry only transient failures, cap attempts, use exponential backoff with jitter and enforce a retry budget. Never retry non-idempotent side effects without an idempotency key. A retry storm can multiply load precisely when a dependency is least able to handle it.

Use circuit breakers to stop repeatedly calling a failing dependency. A simple breaker has CLOSED, OPEN and HALF_OPEN states: calls flow normally when closed; after a failure threshold the breaker opens for a cooldown; then one or a small number of probes test recovery. Bulkheads cap concurrency and queue capacity per dependency or tenant. Backpressure rejects or delays work before memory, connections and token budgets are exhausted.

Plan safe degraded modes. If a model provider is down, a service might return a clearly labeled cached answer within its freshness policy, a retrieval-only result with citations and no generated synthesis, or a retryable unavailable response. Do not silently fabricate a response or claim a tool action succeeded when it did not. If retrieval is unavailable, do not invent citations. Make degradation explicit to the caller and preserve audit evidence.

Finally, test failure and recovery, not just the happy path. Inject timeouts, 429/5xx responses, queue saturation, slow streaming, duplicate side effects and circuit-breaker half-open failures. Measure p50/p95/p99, time-to-first-token, inter-token latency, retry count, queue wait, rejection rate, fallback rate and user-visible success. An SLO is useful only when its measurement and operational response are both trustworthy.
explanation.mentalModel: User journey → explicit SLI and denominator → SLO target and error budget → burn-rate alert → bounded deadlines/retries → breaker/bulkhead/backpressure → safe degraded mode → failure and recovery tests.
limitations: A single availability SLI cannot represent correctness, relevance, safety, freshness or user satisfaction for an AI application.
Percentiles depend on sample size, windowing and aggregation; never average service p95 values to derive end-to-end p95.
Error-budget calculations are only as trustworthy as event eligibility, deduplication and instrumentation.
Retries can worsen overload and duplicate side effects; they need deadlines, retry budgets and idempotency.
Circuit breakers can oscillate or block healthy traffic if thresholds, cooldowns and probe limits are poorly tuned.
A simulator demonstrates policy behavior but does not model real network variance, provider quotas, distributed clocks or production capacity.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: A household has a monthly electricity budget and a backup plan. If usage spikes, you stop optional appliances before the main breaker trips. A circuit breaker protects the system, while a safe backup light keeps essential functions available without pretending everything is normal.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: For 1,000 eligible requests and a 99.5% availability SLO, the allowed failures are 1,000 × (1 − 0.995) = 5. If 5 requests fail, the budget is fully consumed. If 10 fail, 10/5 = 2.0, or 200% budget consumption. If a recent window has a 2% failure ratio, burn rate is 2%/0.5% = 4x.
explanation.productionImpact: Define SLIs from user-visible outcomes, publish SLOs and error budgets, alert on multi-window burn rates, propagate deadlines, bound retries, protect side effects with idempotency, isolate dependencies with breakers and bulkheads, and provide honest degraded modes. Run outage and recovery drills before production incidents.

useCase.scenario: Operate a RAG-agent API that depends on a model provider, vector database, MCP tools and asynchronous indexing. Define user-centered reliability targets, measure budget consumption, prevent retry storms and provide safe degraded behavior during provider and retrieval outages.

constraints: Measure user-visible requests with an explicit denominator.
Do not exclude real dependency failures from availability merely because they are external.
Use one end-to-end deadline and allocate downstream budgets from remaining time.
Retry only transient failures and cap attempts, backoff and total retry budget.
Use idempotency keys for side-effecting operations.
Open breakers and apply backpressure before resource exhaustion.
Fallbacks must be labeled, safe, fresh and honest about missing capabilities.

Safe fallback or explicit unavailable response
useCase.successMetric: The service meets its declared SLO under normal load, avoids cascading failure during dependency outages, and returns an explicit safe degraded response without duplicate side effects.

trustBoundaries: SLI events are validated and deduplicated before they affect error budgets.
External provider status is a dependency signal, not proof of user-visible success or failure by itself.
Retries and circuit-breaker state are server-owned policy; callers cannot raise budgets arbitrarily.
Fallback content must obey freshness, tenant ACL and safety policy.
On-call overrides and error-budget exceptions are scoped, time-bound and audited.
failurePaths: Missing denominator or invalid event: exclude only under a documented eligibility rule and alert on telemetry gaps.
Provider 429/5xx: apply bounded retry with jitter, respect Retry-After where available and open breaker after threshold.
Slow provider: propagate remaining deadline and cancel work after expiry.
Queue saturation: reject or defer with backpressure before exhausting memory and connections.
Breaker half-open probe fails: reopen cooldown and limit probe concurrency.
Model outage: use fresh authorized cache, retrieval-only with citations or explicit unavailable response.
Tool side effect times out: query operation state using idempotency key before retrying.

stages.title: Measure the SLI
stages.narration: Count eligible requests and classify user-visible success and latency against the agreed threshold.
stages.transformation: Compute availability and latency compliance from explicit denominators.

stages.title: Calculate error budget
stages.narration: A 99.5% target permits five bad events out of one thousand.

stages.title: Detect burn rate
stages.narration: A 2% recent failure ratio against a 0.5% budget rate burns at 4x.
stages.transformation: Divide observed bad ratio by target error ratio.

stages.title: Bound retries and deadlines
stages.narration: A provider timeout consumes the remaining deadline; retries are capped and jittered.
stages.transformation: Apply attempt, backoff and retry-budget limits.

stages.title: Open circuit breaker
stages.narration: Repeated failures open the provider breaker and stop calls during cooldown.
stages.transformation: CLOSED → OPEN; later allow a controlled HALF_OPEN probe.

stages.title: Safe fallback and recovery
stages.narration: Return fresh authorized cache, retrieval-only evidence or explicit unavailable status; probe recovery before closing the breaker.
stages.transformation: Select safe degraded mode and evaluate recovery probe.

workedExample.problem: A RAG-agent API handles 1,000 eligible requests. 995 are successful and within the availability definition; p95 latency is 1.8 seconds against a 2-second target. A recent short window has 2% failures while the SLO allows 0.5% failures.
workedExample.input: Eligible requests=1000; good requests=995; p95=1800 ms; latency target=2000 ms; SLO availability=99.5%; recent failure ratio=2%.

steps.reasoning: Good eligible requests divided by total eligible requests equals 995/1000.
The measured p95 of 1.8 seconds is below the 2-second target.
steps.result: The p95 latency target is met.

steps.reasoning: A 99.5% SLO permits 0.5% bad requests; 1000 × 0.005 equals five.
steps.result: Allowed failures are five requests; the observed five consume 100% of this window's budget.

steps.reasoning: Observed failure ratio 2% divided by allowed error ratio 0.5% equals four.
steps.result: Recent burn rate is 4x and should trigger the configured rapid-burn alert.

steps.reasoning: Propagate the remaining request deadline, cap transient retries and open the provider breaker after the threshold.
steps.result: The request does not create an unbounded retry storm or exhaust shared capacity.

steps.reasoning: If authorized cache is fresh, serve it with a degraded label; otherwise return retrieval-only evidence or explicit unavailable status.
steps.result: No fabricated answer or unconfirmed tool side effect is returned.

workedExample.expectedOutput: Availability is exactly 99.5%, p95 latency meets the 2-second target, the five-event error budget is fully consumed, and a 4x burn-rate signal requires investigation. Provider failures are contained by bounded retries and a breaker, with an honest safe fallback.

implementations.expectedResult: Offline simulator calculates availability, latency compliance, error budgets and burn rates; models bounded retry schedules, circuit-breaker transitions and safe fallback selection.
Production guide defines user-centered SLI/SLOs, alert windows, deadlines, retry budgets, idempotency, bulkheads, backpressure and failure drills.

failures.name: SLI denominator excludes real failures
failures.symptom: Dashboard reports high availability while users see dependency failures and timeouts.
failures.rootCause: Eligibility rules silently exclude external-provider failures, retries or cancellations that were user-visible.
failures.recovery: Define eligible events at the user boundary, document exclusions and test numerator/denominator accounting.
failures.regressionTest: A real provider timeout remains a bad eligible event while only documented invalid traffic is excluded.

failures.name: Retry storm amplifies provider outage
failures.symptom: Provider request volume rises while the provider is already returning 429/503.
failures.rootCause: Unbounded retries, synchronized backoff or retries at multiple layers multiply attempts.
failures.recovery: Use capped attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, Retry-After, a shared retry budget and circuit breaker.
failures.regressionTest: A failing dependency cannot exceed the configured attempts or retry budget.

failures.name: Timeout budget resets downstream
failures.symptom: A request exceeds its end-to-end deadline after each service applies its own full timeout.
failures.rootCause: Each dependency receives a fresh timeout instead of remaining request time.
failures.recovery: Propagate one deadline and derive each call timeout from remaining budget.
failures.regressionTest: A downstream call is not started when the remaining deadline is exhausted.

failures.name: Side effect repeated after timeout
failures.symptom: A payment, write or tool action happens twice after a retry.
failures.rootCause: Caller assumes timeout means the remote operation did not execute.
failures.recovery: Use an idempotency key and query durable operation state before retrying.
failures.regressionTest: Duplicate operation key returns the original outcome without a second side effect.

failures.name: Circuit breaker flaps or blocks recovery
failures.symptom: Breaker repeatedly opens and closes or never probes a recovered provider.
failures.rootCause: Thresholds, cooldown and half-open probe concurrency are poorly configured.
failures.recovery: Use a stable failure window, bounded half-open probes and explicit success/failure transitions.
failures.regressionTest: Failed probe reopens the breaker; successful probe closes it.

failures.name: Fallback fabricates missing capability
failures.symptom: The service invents citations or reports a tool action as completed during an outage.
failures.rootCause: Fallback path generates a normal-looking response without the unavailable dependency's evidence.
failures.recovery: Use only fresh authorized cache, retrieval-only evidence with clear labeling, or explicit unavailable status.
failures.regressionTest: When retrieval is down and cache is stale, the fallback is SAFE_UNAVAILABLE.

failures.name: Queue or worker saturation
failures.symptom: Latency and memory usage rise while backlog grows without bound.
failures.rootCause: No queue capacity, concurrency isolation, admission control or backpressure exists.
failures.recovery: Bound queue size and per-dependency concurrency; reject or defer before shared resources are exhausted.
failures.regressionTest: At capacity, new work is rejected with a retryable overload outcome and memory remains bounded.

practice.guided: Run the reliability simulator with 1,000 requests, 995 good outcomes and a 99.5% target. Calculate the five-event budget and 4x burn-rate scenario, then inject provider failures and observe retry and circuit-breaker states.
practice.independent: Add a second SLI for time-to-first-token and a separate quality SLI for citation correctness. Define their denominators and windows, then prove a fast but incorrect answer does not count as a successful task.
practice.realWorld: Design SLOs and runbooks for a production RAG-agent API. Include availability, p95 latency, queue wait, TTFT, tool success, freshness and task-quality indicators. Define burn-rate alerts, error-budget policy, deadline propagation, retry budgets and degraded modes.

Calculate availability and latency SLIs using explicit eligibility rules.
Compute error budget, remaining budget and short/long-window burn rate.

scenarioQuiz.question: A 99.5% availability SLO permits what failure ratio?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: The allowed error ratio is one minus the SLO target: 1 − 0.995 = 0.005, or 0.5%.

scenarioQuiz.question: What is the error budget for 1,000 events at 99.5%?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Allowed bad events equal total events multiplied by the error ratio: 1000 × 0.005 = 5.

scenarioQuiz.question: Why use a shared end-to-end deadline?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Each downstream operation receives only the remaining time, preventing serial calls from each consuming a full fresh timeout.

scenarioQuiz.question: What should a circuit breaker do after repeated failures?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: The OPEN state contains dependency failure and allows recovery time before a controlled HALF_OPEN probe.

scenarioQuiz.question: What is the safest fallback when retrieval is down and cache is stale?
scenarioQuiz.explanation: Without authorized fresh evidence, the service must not fabricate citations or claim unavailable capabilities succeeded.

rubric.evidence: Defines eligible events, good/bad outcomes, latency thresholds and distinct quality/freshness indicators.
Calculates allowed failures, budget consumption and burn rate with correct windows and denominator.
Propagates deadlines, caps retries/backoff and uses idempotency for writes.
Demonstrates circuit breaker, bulkhead/backpressure and honest safe fallback during outages.
Runs outage/recovery tests and maps burn-rate signals to actionable incident/release decisions.

evidence: Availability and latency SLI calculations match the synthetic request set.
Error budget and burn rate are calculated correctly.
Retries remain bounded and idempotent side effects are not duplicated.
Circuit breaker transitions and recovery probes are correct.
Fallback never invents citations or claims unavailable tool success.
Runbook identifies alert, owner, mitigation and recovery evidence.

codeWalkthrough.lines: eligible = [event for event in events if eligibility_policy.includes(event)]
codeWalkthrough.explanation: Define the SLI denominator at the user boundary and document exactly which events are eligible.
Compute the ratio of user-visible good events to all eligible events; dependency failures remain visible.
Translate the SLO target into an allowed number of bad events for the measurement window.
Compare the current failure ratio with the allowed error ratio to estimate how quickly the budget is being consumed.
Propagate one end-to-end deadline and give downstream calls only the remaining time.
Do not continue calling a dependency that has crossed its failure threshold; choose an explicit safe degraded path.
Use a durable idempotency record for side effects and cap transient retries within the request and service retry budgets.
